The application of Augmented Reality (AR) in nursing education offers significant potential for interactive learning, yet a gap exists between development in wealthy nations and implementation in developing regions like the ASEAN area. In countries such as the Philippines and Thailand, budget constraints hinder the adoption of high-tech medical simulations. This exploratory study sought to address this by reviewing existing AR initiatives, identifying affordable development tools, and creating an AR prototype containing Open Educational Resources (OER) for English nursing communication.

The researchers developed a "talking comic strip" prototype using CraftAR, a tool selected for its free license and drag-and-drop interface suitable for non-programmers. The prototype integrated nursing-written scripts, illustrated comic strips, and recorded audio. Evaluation via a usability survey yielded an average System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 68.5937, which exceeds the global mean of 68, indicating relative usability. Students responded favorably, providing high average ratings for the material being better than printed media alone, the enhancement of their learning experience, and the recommendation of the material to training institutions.

The study concludes that AR is accessible to budget-constrained implementers in developing ASEAN countries through free, user-friendly tools. The research suggests that the digital divide in nursing education can be bridged using OER and accessible authoring tools. Future studies should evaluate new AR tools and focus on improving usability, sustainability, and accessibility.

In the study "Validity Testing of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) Survey as a Tool for Student Evaluation of Teaching and Learning in a Fully Online Philippine University," Roja Rivera and Rita Ramos investigate whether the CoI Survey is a suitable Student Evaluation of Teaching (SET) instrument for a fully online university. The researchers note that tools designed for face-to-face instruction often fail to capture the unique pedagogical nuances of online learning, where the instructor's role shifts toward facilitation.

Grounded in the CoI framework—which emphasizes cognitive, social, and teaching presence—the researchers conducted a pilot test with 714 students. Using Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), the study found that the original three-factor model did not fit the specific university context. Instead, EFA identified a four-factor structure: Cognitive Presence, Teaching Presence, Social Presence, and a new factor, Design and Organization. After removing three items that exhibited cross-loading issues, the resulting 31-item model yielded satisfactory fit measures, accounted for 75.5% of the overall variance, and demonstrated high internal consistency.

The researchers conclude that the modified 31-item version is an acceptable tool for evaluating teaching effectiveness. However, they caution that the survey is most valid when applied to courses functioning as a "true" community of inquiry. Because the university utilizes a "guided independent study" mode, some courses may lack the collaborative depth required for the CoI framework to serve as a fair assessment.
